rounds.dominant_cluster: Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: DiseaseClass (Label Mismatch)
rounds.principle: - **IF** a noun phrase is headed by a **generic pathology term** (e.g., a broad disease-process head) but the **full mention is used referentially** to denote an **instantiated diagnosis** or a **contextually narrowed subtype**—signaled by restrictive modifiers or by patient-case, manifestation, association, or etiologic/anatomic context—**THEN** label it **SpecificDisease**; **this does NOT apply** when the same phrase is used **generically, taxonomically, or definitionally** to describe the disease category in general rather than a particular diagnosed condition, in which case label it **DiseaseClass**.
rounds.insight:
- **Pattern Insight**
  - **Pattern Name**: Context-dependent diagnosis hidden behind a generic pathology head
  - **Confusion Trigger**: The mention’s **head noun is a broad disease-process term**—*deficiency, vasculitis, arthritis, infection*—so the model defaults to **DiseaseClass**, even when the full phrase is being used to denote a **specific diagnosed condition/subtype** in context.
  - **Contrastive Evidence**: The true positives mostly contain **overtly lexicalized disease names or conventional subtype labels** such as *Coats disease, Sjogren-Larsson syndrome, ovarian cancer, retinal telangiectasis*. Those phrases signal specificity internally. In the error cases, specificity must be inferred from **clinical/etiologic context** or light modifiers: *PAH deficiencies*, *cutaneous vasculitis*, *Chronic neisserial infection*, or a patient-presentation frame like *presenting with fever, arthritis, and cutaneous vasculitis*.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed)**: If a broad pathology noun is used **referentially** to name an **instantiated diagnosis or etiologically/anatomically constrained subtype**—especially in patient-case, association, or manifestation contexts—label it **SpecificDisease**. Use **DiseaseClass** only when the same noun is used **taxonomically/definitionaly** to denote a general class rather than a particular disease mention.

guideline_after.text: > Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development (so-called retinal telangiectasis).

rounds.dominant_cluster: Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: SpecificDisease (Span Boundary Error)
rounds.principle: - **IF** a candidate **SpecificDisease** appears inside an expanded noun phrase built on a disease-denoting head noun, **THEN** annotate the **smallest contiguous span that still independently identifies the disease**, keeping a post-head complement only when it is **argumentally necessary** to specify an otherwise generic head, and excluding peripheral modifiers or prepositional material that merely add descriptive information such as degree, state, inheritance/carrier status, extent, or anatomical location; **this does NOT apply** when the modifier or complement is **lexically part of the established disease name** or is **required to distinguish the disease referent** rather than merely describe it.
rounds.insight:
- **Pattern Insight**
  - **Pattern Name**: Expanded NP boundary confusion around disease heads
  - **Confusion Trigger**: The mention sits inside a larger noun phrase built on a generic disease head like **disease** or **deficiency**, with nearby **non-core modifiers** before or after it—e.g., premodifiers like **complete / heterozygous** or post-head PPs like **of the retina**. This makes the model drift on span boundaries because the whole NP looks medically cohesive.
  - **Contrastive Evidence**: The true positives are mostly **self-contained disease names** or abbreviations—e.g., **Coats disease**, **Sjogren-Larsson syndrome**, **ovarian cancer**, **SLS**—where there is no hard decision about trimming surrounding descriptive material. The discrepancy cases are harder because the disease mention is **embedded inside an expanded descriptive NP**.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed)**: Select the **minimal disease-denoting span**.  
    - **Include** a following complement only when it is **semantically required** to identify a generic head: e.g., **deficiency of C7**, **deficiency of the seventh component of complement**.  
    - **Exclude** surrounding descriptors that add status, extent, carrier state, or localization but do not define the disease itself: e.g., **complete**, **heterozygous**, and in a self-sufficient name like **Coats' disease**, exclude the attached locator **of the retina**.

guideline_after.text: > Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development (so-called retinal telangiectasis).

rounds.principle: - **IF** a noun phrase in a definitional, characterization, or causal/etiologic context denotes an **abnormal clinical or pathological state**—even when its head is a generic state/process/symptom noun rather than a canonical disease label—**THEN** annotate it as **DiseaseClass**; **do not apply this rule** when the phrase refers only to a normal biological process, a molecular/substance entity or level, or an isolated descriptive finding that is **not** presented as a pathological condition of the patient/disorder.
rounds.insight:
- **Pattern Insight**
  - **Pattern Name**: Compositional pathological-state phrases without explicit disease-name lexemes
  - **Confusion Trigger**: The missed mentions are **descriptive phenotype/pathophysiology NPs**—e.g., headed by generic state/process words or symptom terms like **“development,” “deficiency,” “spasticity”**—often inside definitional frames such as **“is characterized by …”** or **“results in …”**. Because they lack overt disease cues like *disease/syndrome/cancer/disorder*, the model defaults to **O**.
  - **Contrastive Evidence**: The true positives are mostly **canonical disease names** or fixed clinical labels with strong disease signaling, such as **“ovarian cancer,” “Coats disease,” “fragile X syndrome,” “autosomal recessive disorder,” “retinal telangiectasis.”** Even **“mental retardation”** behaves like a lexicalized clinical condition, whereas the discrepancy cases require interpreting a **compositional abnormality description** as a DiseaseClass.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed)**: If a noun phrase appears in a **disease-defining or etiologic context** and denotes an **abnormal clinical/pathological state**—including symptom nouns and phrases like **“abnormal X development,” “deficiency of Y,”** or coordinated features like **“spasticity”**—label it **DiseaseClass** **even when no explicit disease-head word is present**. The key distinction is **pathological-state meaning in a characterization frame**, not the presence of a canonical disease keyword.

guideline_after.text: > Deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase
- In “deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase,” the phrase is **not** annotated because it refers to enzyme activity rather than a disease/pathological-state mention.

guideline_after.text: > Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development (so-called retinal telangiectasis).

- This also excludes mechanistic process descriptions such as “retinal angiogenesis,” “retinal vascular development,” “DNA demethylation,” or “gene reactivation” when they are discussed as processes rather than as disease/pathological-state mentions.

rounds.principle: - **IF** a noun phrase is headed by a deficit/absence nominalization or reduced-function expression and takes a complement naming a **specific molecular entity** (e.g., an enzyme, gene, or protein), **and** the phrase is used in a disease-denoting frame such as definition, causation, characterization, or responsibility for a clinical condition, **THEN** annotate the whole phrase as **SpecificDisease**; **DO NOT** apply this rule when the same wording refers only to an isolated biochemical finding, mechanistic description, or laboratory abnormality rather than the disorder itself.
rounds.insight:
- **Pattern Insight**
  - **Pattern Name**: Deficiency-headed disease paraphrases
  - **Confusion Trigger**: The mention is a noun phrase headed by **“deficiency” / “deficient activity”** plus an enzyme/gene/protein complement (e.g., “deficiency of hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase”), so it looks like a mechanistic abnormality rather than a disease name.
  - **Contrastive Evidence**: The true positives mostly contain **canonical disease-head lexemes** such as *syndrome, disease, cancer,* or an established pathology term (*telangiectasis*). Those overt disease heads cue the model correctly, whereas the discrepancy cases lack them and are expressed as biochemical-defect descriptions.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed)**: When a phrase is **headed by deficiency/deficient activity** and its complement is a **specific enzyme/gene/protein**, treat it as **SpecificDisease** if it is used to denote the disorder/clinical condition itself—especially in disease-defining frames like **“caused by,” “characterized by,”** or **“responsible for.”** Do not require an explicit disease word for such metabolic/enzyme-deficiency mentions.
